generalfeedback:
To find \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) when \[y=\cosh^{-1}\left(\sqrt{{{CT:0}} {{CT:1}} + {{CT:2}}}\right) .\]

In order to solve this problem we will have to use the chain rule \(\frac{df}{d{{CT:1}}}=\frac{df}{dg} \cdot\frac{dg}{dh}\cdot\frac{dh}{d{{CT:1}}}\)  as follows:

Define \(h({{CT:1}})={{CT:0}}{{CT:1}}+{{CT:2}}\), \(g(h) = \sqrt{h} = h^{\frac{1}{2}}\) and \(f(g)=\cosh^{-1}\left(g\right)\).

So, \[\begin{array}{rcl}\displaystyle \frac{d}{d{{CT:1}}}\left(\cosh^{-1}\left(\sqrt{{{CT:0}} {{CT:1}} + {{CT:2}}}\right)\right) &\displaystyle =&\displaystyle \frac{df}{dg}\cdot \frac{dg}{dh}\cdot \frac{dh}{d{{CT:1}}} \\ &\displaystyle =&\displaystyle \frac{d}{dg}(\cosh^{-1}\left(g\right))\cdot\frac{d}{dh}(h^{\frac{1}{2}})\cdot \frac{d}{d{{CT:1}}}({{CT:0}} {{CT:1}}+{{CT:2}}) \\ &\displaystyle =&\displaystyle \frac{1}{ \sqrt{g^2-1}}\cdot\frac{1}{2}(h^{-\frac{1}{2}})\cdot {{CT:0}} \\ &\displaystyle =&\displaystyle \frac{1}{ \sqrt{h-1}}\cdot\frac{{CT:0}}{2 \sqrt{h}} \\&\displaystyle =&\displaystyle {{CT:3}}\end{array}\]

on_true.feedback: To differentiate a function of a function, you must use the chain rule! It is \[\frac{df}{dg} \cdot\frac{dg}{dx}.\]
You appear to have applied the chain rule incorrectly. It is \[\frac{df}{dg} \cdot\frac{dg}{dx}.\]
